wording: A competing pattern to P87's British rise: in the US, intergenerational mobility declined substantially over the past 150 y, but more slowly than previously thought, with father-son occupational rank-rank correlations rising from about 0.17 (1830 cohort) to 0.27 (1900) and 0.32 (1980), mostly before 1900 and largely through the farm-to-factory shift; net of farm origins relative mobility was largely stable, while absolute upward mobility rose for cohorts born before 1900 and fell after 1940. P96: absolute mobility changed more over time than relative mobility. Audit (SOC iteration 8): 0.01 per decade, 165 years and 16 cohorts follow from its endpoints; two-thirds of the correlation rise came by 1900.

wording: In the agent's rank toy (70 equal occupations, P96's 7.5-point threshold), raising the father-son correlation from 0.17 to 0.32 cuts the upward share only from 41.3% to 39.8%, whereas shifting sons up by 0.3 SD (structural upgrading) raises it to 49.9% (down 30.2%) with the rank correlation unchanged (0.309 vs 0.308) and downgrading by 0.2 SD reverses it (up 33.4%, down 46.4%): absolute mobility tracks structure, relative mobility tracks inheritance, as P96 and P87 both argue. Rank correlations match (6/pi) asin(rho/2); with a 15-point threshold only 35.7% stay (pre-registered 'more than half stay' not supported). QPM calibration: 1901 52% between scales 1.25 and 1.3 (51.2%); 2001 67% at 0.55 (67.2%); 1974 64% near 0.9 (63.7%).
counterevidence_limits: Toy statuses are bivariate normal with equal-sized occupations; QPM scaling is the agent's model.
